title: An Image Is Worth 16×16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
authors: Alexey Dosovitskiy, Lucas Beyer, Alexander Kolesnikov, Dirk Weissenborn, Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, Matthias Minderer, Georg Heigold, Sylvain Gelly, Jakob Uszkoreit, Neil Houlsby

pages.title: Pure Transformers, no convolutions, beat CNNs at scale

blocks.html: Convolutional networks had dominated image recognition since 2012. Their inductive biases — translation equivariance, locality — match natural images well, and they were the natural answer to 'how do you process pixels.'

Vision Transformer (ViT) proposes throwing all that away: cut an image into fixed-size patches, treat each patch as a 'word,' and apply a standard Transformer encoder (the same one from Attention Is All You Need). No convolutions. No image-specific inductive biases.

When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

Key empirical finding: at small data scales (ImageNet alone), CNNs win because their inductive biases help. At large data scales (JFT-300M, 14M+ ImageNet-21k), ViT wins — the model learns its own priors from data and ends up generalizing better.

pages.title: Turning an image into a sequence

blocks.html: An image $x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ is reshaped into a sequence of flattened patches $x_p \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (P^2 \cdot C)}$, where $P$ is the patch size and $N = HW/P^2$ is the number of patches. For 224×224 images with P=16, that's 196 patches.

Each patch is linearly projected to a $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional embedding by a single learned matrix (one $P^2 C \times d_{\text{model}}$ projection, applied to every patch). This is equivalent to a single convolution with kernel size $P$ and stride $P$ — but conceptually it's just 'tokenize the image.'
A learnable [CLS] token is prepended (borrowed from BERT). Its output state after the encoder is used as the image representation for classification.
Learned positional embeddings are added to all tokens. The paper experiments with 2D-aware positional embeddings but finds standard 1D learned positions work as well.

After tokenization, the architecture is identical to a standard Transformer encoder: alternating multi-head self-attention and MLP blocks, each preceded by LayerNorm (pre-norm variant), with residual connections. No image-specific machinery.
Variants: ViT-Base (12 layers, 12 heads, $d = 768$, 86M params), ViT-Large (24/16/1024, 307M), ViT-Huge (32/16/1280, 632M). Patch sizes 16 or 32.
Hybrid model: alternatively, use a small ResNet to extract feature maps, then patchify the feature map instead of raw pixels. The hybrid wins at small scale; pure ViT wins as data grows.

pages.title: Pre-training data matters more than anything

items: JFT-300M (300M images, Google's internal dataset): ViT-H clearly wins — 88.55% on ImageNet, 90.72% on CIFAR-100, with less pre-training compute than CNN baselines.

blocks.html: The figure on page 6 (the famous 'BiT vs ViT' curve) makes the data-scale story explicit: ViT's accuracy grows faster with pre-training data than CNN's. The crossover sits around 100M images.
Several analyses from §5 of the paper:

items: Patch projection first principal components look like Gabor-style edge detectors — ViT rediscovers CNN-like early features by itself.
Positional embeddings learn 2D structure: nearby patches end up with similar embeddings even though the layer is 1D-positional.

Attention distance (analogous to CNN receptive field): in early layers, some heads attend locally and others globally. CNNs are forced to start local. ViT learns when local matters and when global does.

blocks.html: Before ViT, vision and NLP architectures were largely separate research traditions. After ViT, they converged. Today the same Transformer block underlies image classification, detection (DETR, Swin), segmentation, video understanding, multimodal models (CLIP, Flamingo, Gemini), diffusion models (DiT), and protein folding (AlphaFold's evoformer).

The bigger lesson: architectural inductive biases matter less as data and compute scale. Given enough of both, a general-purpose model that learns its biases from data tends to beat a specialized model whose biases were hand-designed.
